title: Autosave changed the design question

children.text: AstraPay KYC used to follow a fixed sequence. Users completed one section, went through the required guide, and moved on to the next step.

Once Autosave entered development, the product question became bigger than saving progress. If KTP and Selfie could persist independently, users should also be able to return without losing work and finish whatever was still incomplete.

callout: The question shifted from “how do we save progress?” to “how flexible should KYC become once progress can persist?”

title: Two ways to build Autosave
description: Both concepts supported saved progress, but they organized the experience differently.

left.label: Flow A
left.title: Keep the sequence
left.description: KYC stayed ordered. The guide remained mandatory before users could move into the next step.
left.alt: Flow A KYC with a fixed sequence and mandatory guide
left.note: Autosave sits inside the existing linear flow.

right.label: Flow B
right.title: Make Review the hub
right.description: Users could see progress from Review, start with either KTP or Selfie, then return to finish the remaining section.
right.alt: Flow B KYC with Review as a flexible progress hub
right.note: Guidance remained available without being forced.

title: More flexibility does not automatically mean easier

children.text: Flow B gave users more control, but that also introduced more choice. We needed to know whether the extra flexibility helped without making KYC harder to understand.
The decision therefore could not come from design preference alone. Both flows were tested as usable end-to-end experiences.

callout: The goal was not to find the more modern-looking flow. It was to see whether flexibility introduced a usability cost.

title: Randomized usability test
description: The study ran unmoderated in Maze and was followed by a post-test survey.

alt: Materials and setup for the KYC Autosave randomized usability test

title: The inferential results did not produce a winner

children.text: SUS and total misclicks showed no statistically significant difference between Flow A and Flow B. Several perception measures, including ease and confidence, followed the same pattern.
That result mattered because it set a clear boundary on the claim. The evidence did not support saying that Flow B was statistically better.

callout: A non-significant result does not make the experiment useless. It means descriptive signals should stay descriptive while the decision looks at the rest of the evidence.

title: The decision came from the full pattern

children.text: Once the inferential results showed no clear winner, I returned to the descriptive data and open-ended feedback. Flow B showed a lower misclick trend and more stable confidence.

User feedback also leaned toward a structure that made progress visible and let people return to unfinished KYC sections. Those signals were not enough to claim statistical superiority, but they still mattered when read alongside the product goal.
At a system level, Flow B also fit Autosave better. Saving sections independently would deliver much less value if users were still forced through the same sequence as before.

callout: Flow B was selected because it introduced no meaningful usability penalty and matched the behavior Autosave was meant to enable, not because it “won the A/B test.”

title: What the study could and could not support
description: Keeping this distinction visible made the product decision useful without overstating the research.

left.label: Not supported
left.title: Flow B is proven better
left.description: The study found no significant difference in SUS or total misclicks. There was no basis for calling Flow B the statistical winner.

right.label: Supported
right.title: Flow B is a reasonable baseline
right.description: There was no meaningful usability penalty. Descriptive patterns, user feedback, and fit with the Autosave model gave enough reason to move forward with Flow B.
right.note: The decision used the full body of evidence.

title: Turning the experiment into product behavior

children.text: Flow B became the foundation for KYC Autosave. Review acted as the progress hub, while KTP and Selfie could be completed without depending on a rigid order.
Once a section was completed, progress persisted when users returned to Review. Individual sections could also be corrected or retaken before final submission without restarting the entire flow.

callout: Autosave stopped being only a persistence feature. It became the foundation for a KYC flow that could be left, resumed, and corrected section by section.

alt: Flow B selected as the implementation baseline for KYC Autosave

title: What the evidence actually established
description: The direct study result is separated from the conversion movement seen across the broader KYC improvement period.

metrics.label: peak KYC uplift
metrics.context: observed during the broader KYC improvement period

metrics.label: baseline uplift
metrics.note: Other KYC changes, including homepage copy, were also live.

title: The impact needs a clear attribution boundary

children.text: Across the broader KYC improvement period, conversion reached its highest level, with peak uplift around 11% and the baseline settling roughly 5% above the previous period.
Autosave was not the only change in market. The KYC homepage copy was also updated, so I do not attribute the full uplift to Flow B.

The study established something narrower and more defensible: a more flexible structure could be introduced without a meaningful usability penalty and then serve as the foundation for the KYC flow that followed.

callout: Strong evidence does not always end in a single winning number. Sometimes its value is making the next production decision safer.

title: A non-significant result can still change the product decision

children.text: This experiment changed how I interpret usability studies when the statistics do not produce a winner. The job is not to find a story that makes one design look better anyway.
A better approach is to keep the claim boundary intact, then ask whether descriptive data, user feedback, and system needs still provide a reasonable basis for the product decision.
